researchQuestion: Which RNA-mediated silencing effects and bacterial repeat-associated immune mechanisms could become general sequence-specific genome-targeting tools?

corpus.title: [SYNTHETIC] Injected antisense and sense RNA strands both suppress target-gene expression in C. elegans
corpus.abstract: [SYNTHETIC] Injection of either antisense or sense RNA into C. elegans suppresses corresponding target genes in a concentration-dependent manner; the effect spreads between tissues and persists for a generation, suggesting an amplifying cellular pathway.

corpus.title: [SYNTHETIC] Clustered short palindromic repeats in prokaryotic genomes: conserved pattern without assigned function
corpus.abstract: [SYNTHETIC] Tandem short repeats separated by conserved spacers appear across E. coli and archaeal genomes; adjacent gene families encode conserved predicted nucleases with no experimentally assigned role.

corpus.title: [SYNTHETIC] Zinc-finger nucleases direct sequence-specific genome modification in cultured cells
corpus.abstract: [SYNTHETIC] Fusing engineered zinc-finger DNA-binding domains to a nuclease domain yields double-strand cuts at chosen genomic loci; specificity is limited by finger-domain context effects.

corpus.title: [SYNTHETIC] Transposon-mediated insertional mutagenesis: coverage, footprinting, and limits
corpus.abstract: [SYNTHETIC] Transposon mutagenesis saturates bacterial and yeast genomes but leaves footprint mutations and exhibits insertion-site bias that complicates clean genome engineering.

targets.statement: Double-stranded RNA triggers sequence-specific gene silencing (RNA interference) in animals (Fire et al., Nature, 1998).
Cas9 guided by a single engineered RNA cleaves arbitrary DNA targets, enabling programmable genome editing (Jinek et al., Science, 2012).

hypotheses.statement: Double-stranded RNA mediates sequence-specific gene silencing across animal cell lineages.
hypotheses.mechanism: dsRNA injected into an animal triggers a cellular pathway that degrades mRNA sharing its sequence; the tissue-to-tissue spread and generational persistence reported for sense-strand suppression are explained by a dsRNA intermediate amplified inside the cell.

falsificationMethod.prediction: Purified dsRNA injection leaves target mRNA abundance unchanged (fold change above 2 versus buffer control)

hypotheses.relationToExistingTheory: Unifies the anomalous sense-strand suppression results with classical antisense effects.
alternativeExplanations: Single-strand antisense contamination drives the observed suppression.
observablePredictions: dsRNA is orders of magnitude more potent per molecule than either single strand.
distinguishingObservations: Dose-response separation between purified dsRNA and its denatured strands.
hypotheses.noveltyRelativeToCorpus: Names the actual interfering species and generalizes it across lineages.
assumptions: Purified dsRNA can be delivered intact to target tissues.

hypotheses.statement: Bacterial repeat-associated nuclease systems could be retooled with a single engineered RNA to cut chosen DNA sequences.
hypotheses.mechanism: The conserved nuclease gene family adjacent to the clustered repeats likely acts on foreign DNA guided by repeat-derived transcripts; replacing the spacer-derived segment of that transcript with an engineered sequence would redirect the cut to arbitrary matching genomic sites.

falsificationMethod.prediction: Reconstituted nuclease plus engineered single RNA fails to cut plasmid targets in vitro (cleaved fraction below 0.05)

hypotheses.relationToExistingTheory: Repositions an unexplained prokaryotic repeat system as a programmable nuclease chassis.
alternativeExplanations: The repeat system is a DNA-level repair or partitioning mechanism, not RNA-guided cleavage.
observablePredictions: Cleavage maps to sites complementary to the engineered RNA segment.
distinguishingObservations: Mutation of the nuclease catalytic residues abolishes cutting without altering RNA binding.
hypotheses.noveltyRelativeToCorpus: First proposal in this corpus context to externalize targeting onto an RNA rather than a protein domain.
assumptions: The nuclease accepts non-native guide segments.

hypotheses.statement: Zinc-finger nuclease specificity can be improved by modular assembly of DNA-recognition helices.
hypotheses.mechanism: Independent finger modules bind triplet subsites; array assembly from a modular code reduces the context effects that limit current fusion nucleases.

falsificationMethod.prediction: Modularly assembled arrays exceed a 10 percent off-target cleavage rate at endogenous loci

hypotheses.relationToExistingTheory: Incremental refinement of the protein-based targeting strategy.
alternativeExplanations: Context-dependent finger pairing defeats modular coding.
observablePredictions: Engineered arrays cut designated loci with predictable rates.
distinguishingObservations: Parallel assembly of the same specificity in two scaffolds.
hypotheses.noveltyRelativeToCorpus: Engineering-methods claim within the established zinc-finger paradigm.
assumptions: Triplet recognition is context-free to first order.
risks: Assembly screening cost scales with array length.
